soil-fert-209.title: Guano, the seabird dung that fed the world
soil-fert-209.text: Andean people may have spread seabird droppings from Peru's coastal islands on their fields for as long as 5,000 years. Guano, a word from Quechua, is the accumulated excrement of seabirds or bats, used as fertilizer. It is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium. Both kinds exceed 40% organic matter, and bat guano may hold up to 6% available P2O5. After Alexander von Humboldt studied it in 1802 and Humphry Davy praised the Peruvian kind, guano became popular in Europe in the 19th century. European guano was poorer, its potency leached by high rainfall and humidity. The seabird guano trade played a pivotal role in the rise of modern input-intensive farming. Demand fell rapidly after 1910 with the Haber–Bosch process, but organic food has revived it in the 21st century. The cost is real. Unsustainable mining has destroyed habitat and killed millions of seabirds, and harvesting bat guano can drive bats from their roosts.

soil-fert-215.title: Wood ash, a liming agent from the fireplace
soil-fert-215.text: Burning wood leaves about 6–10% of it behind as ash, a powdery residue made largely of calcium compounds. As a fertilizer it supplies potassium and calcium carbonate, which acts as a liming agent to neutralize acid soils. Calcium carbonate may make up 25% or even 45% of its weight. Ash typically holds 7–33% calcium, 3–10% potassium, 1–2% magnesium and 0.3–1.4% phosphorus. Hotter fires leave less ash and drive off potassium, sulfur and boron. Ash also carries trace heavy metals, such as lead at 2–500 ppm and cadmium at 0.18–60 ppm.

soil-fert-205.title: Biostimulants, neither fertilizer nor pesticide
soil-fert-205.text: Some products help crops grow without being fertilizer or pesticide. These biostimulants are substances, microbial cultures or mixtures used to promote crop growth. A proposed standard definition says they work through emergent properties of their constituents, not merely through known nutrients, growth regulators or protective compounds. Ingredients include humic substances, amino acids, seaweed extracts and chitin derivatives. Living agents include growth-promoting rhizobacteria and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Registered endophytic strains, microbes living inside plants, have improved nutrient use efficiency and stress tolerance in the field. With no agreed definition, as of 2016 no country had a specific regulatory framework for them.

soil-fert-210.title: The Guano Age, when bird droppings ran a treasury
soil-fert-210.text: Peru once funded its state on bird droppings. From 1840 it made guano an exclusive state resource, and the royalties became the country's largest source of revenue. This Guano Age ran from Humboldt's investigations at Callao in 1802 to the War of the Pacific. By 1846, 462,057 tonnes had left Ichaboe Island off Namibia for Britain. Peru's exports peaked above 700,000 tonnes in 1870, though the Chincha Islands were nearly exhausted. The US Guano Islands Act of 1856 let citizens claim unclaimed guano islands, and nearly 100 were annexed. Afterward Chile saltpeter eclipsed guano.

soil-fert-211.title: Liquid manure, from slurry pit to vegetable field
soil-fert-211.text: Post-war tractors changed how farms handle dung. Powerful enough to haul heavy tanks, they let farmers spread liquid manure evenly near plant roots. Liquid manure is a mixture of animal waste and organic matter, sometimes thinned with water, developed in the 20th century as an alternative to fermented manure. A slurry pit can age and concentrate it. Like solid manure, it is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium from the animals' feed. Concentrated animal feeding operations supply most of it spread on US vegetable fields, a route for E. coli O157:H7. Runoff from such operations contaminated wells in the fatal Walkerton outbreak.

soil-fert-216.title: Turning an NPK label into real phosphorus and potassium
soil-fert-216.text: A bag labeled 18-51-20 does not hold 51% phosphorus. Labels give phosphorus as P2O5 and potassium as K2O, so a simple calculation recovers the elements. P2O5 is 43.6% phosphorus by weight, so elemental phosphorus is 0.436 times the P value. K2O is 83% potassium, so elemental potassium is 0.83 times the K value. The N value already gives elemental nitrogen and needs no conversion. That 18-51-20 fertilizer thus holds 18% nitrogen, 22% phosphorus and 17% potassium. Pure potassium chloride, 52% potassium, would read 0-0-63; sylvite, which contains other compounds, usually reads 0-0-60.

soil-fert-207.title: Ecological sanitation: closing the loop from toilet to field
soil-fert-207.text: A toilet can be the first step in growing food. Ecological sanitation aims to reuse human excreta safely in agriculture, closing the nutrient loop between sanitation and farming. It is an approach, not a technology; urine-diverting dry toilets are its most common technology but not the only one. Trials around the world show measurable benefits from treated excreta, especially urine, as fertilizer and soil conditioner. It may also ease a possible phosphorus shortage. One review suggested phosphate collected from urine could meet 22% of total demand. Whether its treatments destroy pathogens safely is still debated, though WHO reuse guidelines with a multiple barrier concept give a common framework.

soil-fert-214.title: Polyhalite, four nutrients from deep under Yorkshire
soil-fert-214.text: The only polyhalite mined lies more than 1,000 m below North Yorkshire, in a layer 260 million years old. Boulby Mine has worked it since 2010. Polyhalite is an evaporite mineral, one left behind by evaporating water, and a hydrated sulfate of potassium, calcium and magnesium. As fertilizer it supplies four nutrients and little chloride: 48% SO3, 14% K2O, 6% MgO and 17% CaO. As a soil amendment it can improve drainage and fertility and help reduce soil acidity.

soil-fert-212.title: Nutrient budgeting, keeping the books on a farm's soil
soil-fert-212.text: A farm can keep accounts for its nutrients as well as its money. Nutrient budgeting compares all the nutrients applied to a farm's soil with all those removed. Inputs include fertilizer, rainfall, brought-in supplements and spread effluent. Outputs include sold stock, crops, milk, meat and wool, plus leaching of nitrate, volatilization and phosphate runoff. A surplus builds up nutrients and the risk of loss; a deficit drains reserves and risks deficiencies and lower yields. Budgets are less exact than financial statements, drawing on yield history, past applications and average removal coefficients. They are a best management practice in the 4R strategy.

soil-fert-217.title: Fertilizer placement: broadcast or banded with the seed
soil-fert-217.text: Where fertilizer goes can strongly affect how much of it a crop takes up. Fertilizer placement is that choice, such as broadcasting over the field or banding with the seed. Broadcast urea beyond what plants use causes nitrous oxide emissions and water pollution. Banding has its own hazard. Hydrolyzing urea creates a toxic high-ammonia zone, so urea fertilizers should not be applied or banded with seed at more than 10–20 kg/ha, depending on the crop. Feeding through irrigation, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-208}}, places nutrients wherever the water goes.

soil-fert-206.title: Diammonium phosphate and its delayed acid twist
soil-fert-206.text: Ammonia meets phosphoric acid, and the product is diammonium phosphate, (NH4)2HPO4, a water-soluble salt used as fertilizer. Its typical NPK rating is 18-46-0: 18% nitrogen, 46% P2O5 and no K2O. Its effect on soil pH reverses with time. At first it raises pH, but over the long term the ground becomes more acidic than before as its ammonium is nitrified. Its solution averages pH 7.5–8. Alkaline chemicals turn its ammonium into ammonia, so the two are incompatible. In air it slowly loses ammonia, and at around 70 °C it breaks down to ammonia and monoammonium phosphate.

soil-fert-213.title: Phosphogypsum, the radioactive leftover of fertilizer acid
soil-fert-213.text: Every ton of phosphoric acid leaves about five tons of waste. That waste is phosphogypsum, a calcium sulfate hydrate, mainly gypsum, left when phosphoric acid for fertilizer is made from phosphate rock. Output reaches an estimated 100 to 280 million tonnes a year. Uranium at 5–10 ppm, thorium and their daughter nuclides make it weakly radioactive, so most is stored indefinitely. Up to 15% is used, partly as a soil amendment. In 1990 the US EPA banned most uses above 10 picocuries of radium-226 per gram. Storage remains controversial. The EPA approved its use in roads in 2020 over environmentalists' objections, then withdrew the rule in 2021.
